en: Next, he addressed Rāhula, commanding him to go inquire after the illness.

While the previous eight individuals were instructed in the methods for clarifying and practicing the Dharma, here, in addressing Rāhula, the Buddha clarifies the method for generating the mind of enlightenment and leaving the household life. Rāhula is the son of the Buddha;
this name means "obscuration" (*āvṛti*), and is also called "non-release. Because he remained in his mother’s womb for six years without emerging, he is named "The Obscured" (*Āvṛta*).
It was due to obstacles and lack of diligence.
For what reason did he remain in the womb for six years without emerging?
It was because of past conditions.
As it is said in the Sūtra:
In a former life, he was once a king; because a śramaṇa sought an audience for six days and he would not look upon him, he received this retribution.
Furthermore, in the distant past, he once blocked a mouse hole; therefore, he receives this retribution.
As the Buddha was about to leave the household life, his father, the King, feared that the national sacrificial rites would be interrupted;
he detained him and would not permit his departure. At that time, the Bodhisattva pointed his finger at the queen’s belly and said to her, “Six years from now, you shall give birth to a son.”
It was exactly as he had said; Rāhula was born six years after the Buddha’s renunciation.
The circumstances of his birth are fully detailed in the sūtras.
By the time the Buddha returned to the palace after attaining enlightenment, Rāhula was approximately five or six years old.

As the Tathāgata was about to arrive, he transformed a thousand bhikṣus so that they all appeared identical to his own form. Rāhula went directly to the Buddha’s location; the Buddha stroked the crown of his head with his hand and led him back to the vihāra, where he commanded Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana to ordain him.

After he had left the household life, he took pleasure in using harsh speech and slandering others by name; at one time, the Buddha admonished him with the Dharma, whereupon he forever ceased beating or reviling others and was free from anger.
The Buddha praised that person for his patience and observance of the precepts, declaring him foremost in secret practice.
He now commands him to inquire after [the Buddha’s] illness; first comes the announcement, followed by the departure.
Within the departure, there is first a general summary, secondly an explanation, and finally a conclusion.
In the commentary, the phrase "the reason why" serves to raise a question regarding what precedes it and introduces what follows.
Below, the text provides a formal analysis in three distinct parts:
first, citing the circumstances by which [the Buddha] was rebuked in the past.
2. From "At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me" onwards, it clarifies the words of his reprimand.
3. From "Thereupon, Vimalakīrti spoke to all those who had already [attained]" onwards, it clarifies the benefit of his reprimand.
At the beginning, "Recalling the Past" indicates the time when [the Buddha] was rebuked.
"Vaiśālī," and so forth, clarifies the matter of the rebuke.
First the question, then the answer.
For what reason do these sons of the elders ask?
They observe that Rāhula has renounced things of great weight, yet they have not yet seen what he has gained; it is for this reason that they ask with wonder.
By saying "the sons of the elders of Vaiśālī," the questioners are identified.
"Come to me," and so forth, clarifies the request for skillful means.
"He asked me," and so forth, indicates the words of inquiry.
"O Rāhula," respectfully addresses the person.
"You are the son of the Buddha"—the inheritance is most sublime.
"He renounced the rank of a Wheel-Turning King"—what was renounced was most weighty.
If that Rāhula had not gone forth into homelessness, he would have become an Iron-Wheel-Turning King, ruling over Jambudvīpa.
Therefore, I now cite this:
"Leaving home to pursue the Way" (chujia wei dao) clarifies what one undertakes.
To establish oneself within the secular world is called having a "home"; to abandon the white robes for the black robes is termed "leaving home to pursue the Way."
"What are the benefits of that renunciation? asks regarding what is attained. "Rāhu" answers below:

"I shall explain for you the merits and benefits of renunciation. This refers to what is taught in the *Pravrajyāguṇa Sūtra*. The sūtra states: "If someone were to kill all sentient beings within the three-thousandfold world system, or gouge out the eyes of the sentient beings of those three thousand worlds, their transgression would be immeasurable."
"The one who leaves the household life possesses far greater merit than that.
Rāhula, you should explain these benefits to him.
From this point downward is the second section, clarifying the words of admonition.
Why was this necessary?
It was because Rāhula and the son of the elder were to be taught to depart correctly from [clinging to] signs; therefore, it was necessary to instruct and reprimand them.
The passage, "Then Vimalakīrti came and said to me," serves as a general heading.
The following section provides a specific exposition; within this exposition, the initial portion is a rebuke.
The section beginning with "Now, as for those who have left the household life" constitutes the correct teaching according to the Dharma.
Within the rebuke, the phrase "one should not speak of the benefits of leaving the household life" constitutes the formal rebuke itself.
The section beginning with "Therefore" provides an explanation, first posing a challenge and subsequently offering a resolution.
The statement, "To have neither benefit nor merit is what constitutes leaving home," cites this to reveal its opposite.
The passage, "Conditioned phenomena may be said to possess benefit and merit," etc., clarifies that the latter is not distinct from the former.
Pleasure is termed "benefit," and goodness is designated as "virtue.

Because Rāhu has abandoned worldly life to become a renunciant, he speaks of pleasure as benefit in contrast to the sufferings of worldly occupations and the like; he speaks of goodness as virtue in contrast to the wrongdoings of improper occupations within that worldly life.

Vimalakīrti takes departure from signs to be "leaving home"; therefore, he says that to have neither benefit nor merit constitutes leaving home, whereas to have benefit and merit is entirely termed being "at home. Since these are subsumed under the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it is said that the conditioned can indeed be described as having benefit and merit.
The above constitutes the rebuke, while the below constitutes the instruction.
Within the instruction, there is first a specific analysis;
from "If one is able" onwards, it serves as a general conclusion and praise.
The separate section has two parts:
first, teaching by means of the previous questions;
second, from "For those who have left the home life, there is neither 'this' nor 'that'" onwards, a general presentation of all the teachings on the dharma for those who have left the home life.
In the first part of the middle section, the phrase "Now, as for those who have left the household life" serves as a general heading.
The phrase "for the sake of unconditioned dharmas" clarifies what they seek; that which is sought is unconditioned nirvana.
The statement, "In unconditioned dharmas there is neither benefit nor virtue," clarifies their source.
In the general teaching below, the term "those who have left the household life" is used as a general heading.
He instructs them through the correct teaching; herein, he first teaches by means of his own practice.
From "subduing the various māras" onwards, he teaches by means of external transformation for the benefit of others.
In the beginning of the middle section, it says, "There is neither that nor this, being free from the sixty-two views," which teaches the source [of these views].
It further says, "There is neither that nor this, nor is there anything in between," which teaches the departure from signs (*nimitta*).
To take the secular life as "this" and the monastic life as "that," with the expedient of renunciation as the "middle" that moves from this toward that—none of these exist here.
Alternatively, one might name birth and death as "this" and the nirvana of severed fetters as "that," with the Noble Path as the "middle"—none of these exist here either.
"Leaving behind the sixty-two views" teaches the removal of emotional attachments.
The sixty-two views will be discussed in detail later.
This teaching is that from which [the path] emerges; the *Nirvāṇa* and other teachings are those into which it enters.

“Abiding in nirvāṇa” generally clarifies that which is entered; it means abiding in the unconditioned nirvāṇa of the dharma-nature, which is precisely what was previously termed “unconditioned dharmas.
“That which is accepted by the wise and practiced by the noble ones” specifically clarifies that which is entered.

The stage prior to nirvāṇa is that which precedes the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), while that which is received by the wise is the stage of the grounds (*bhūmi-stha*) because it is the sphere of activity of the noble ones (*ārya*); therefore, one should abide therein.
Bodhisattvas prior to the grounds are called "wise" because they generate understanding based on the teachings; they are said to "receive" because they accord with faith based on the teachings.
On the ground, those who have attained correct vision are called "sages" (ārya); the sage’s mind dwells within the Dharma and takes its exposition as practice.
Since the *dharmatā*-nirvāṇa serves as the basis for this practice, it is termed the "sphere of practice" (*gocara*).
The former teaching is for one's own practice; the latter teaching is for the benefit of others.
Within this, the initial section first teaches how to subdue Māra;
the section beginning with "Crushing all" and following teaches how to subjugate non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
In the preceding section, "subduing Māra" refers to the person who subdues Māra.
"Delivering beings from the five paths," and so forth, refers to the destruction of Māra’s methods.
Within these methods, there are three [aspects]:
First, to clarify that which is produced: the teaching delivers beings across the five realms of existence.
Hell, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, and devas constitute these five realms.
To eliminate the causes and depart from the effects is what is termed "deliverance."
Second, it clarifies the purification of the five eyes and five powers through the teachings one cultivates.
The five eyes constitute understanding; their meaning is as explained in a separate chapter and should be discussed in full here.
The faculties and powers constitute practice; these five are faith, diligence, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
That which begins as cultivation is called a faculty (*indriya*); that which culminates in completion is called a power (*bala*).
That which the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*) cause one to abandon is taught as being far removed from the activities of Māra.
"Not to afflict others" means not to destroy the goodness of others.
"Free from all various evils" means that one does not personally give rise to transgressions.
"Subduing among the heterodox" and "crushing all heterodox teachers" refer to subduing those of deviant views.
"Transcending the provisional" and so forth refer to the refutation of deviant teachings.
Within this, there are also three parts:
first, clarifying that which is produced;
second, from "internal destruction" onwards, returning to clarify that which is cultivated.
3. From "Detachment from the Multitude" (*li zhong*) onwards, the text again clarifies that which is to be detached from.
Within the preceding section, it clarifies the emergence from afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering;
by transcending provisional designations (*prajñapti*), it clarifies the emergence from suffering.
The retribution of birth and death exists only as a provisional designation; thus it is called a "provisional name" (*prajñapti*).
Because one realizes the truth and abandons [this designation], it is said to be "transcended.
The meaning of provisional names is explained extensively in other chapters; here, I shall briefly analyze it.
The Sūtra states that there are four [distinctions]:
first, birth-and-death is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), whereas nirvāṇa is not provisional.
This is as stated here: because birth-and-death exists as a floating, empty, and provisional designation, it is called a "provisional designation"; nirvāṇa is real, and therefore is not provisional.
Second, *nirvāṇa* is a provisional designation (*prajñapti*), whereas *saṃsāra* is not provisional.
As the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"Nirvāṇa has no name; names are provisionally established for it, therefore it is called a 'provisional designation.'"
The phenomena of birth and death are in reality termed "existence" (*bhava*); therefore, they are not provisional.
Third, both birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are equally provisional designations.
As stated in the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*:
Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are, in their essence, dharmas that exist provisionally through causes and conditions; therefore, they are said to be "provisional.
To apply the designation "provisional" is to speak of them as "provisional names.
Furthermore, because the characteristics of the dharmas of birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are established by means of provisional names, they are called "provisional names."
Fourth, both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not provisional.
When one sets aside names to seek the Dharma, the essence of the Dharma is the suchness (tathatā) of reality; therefore, it is not provisional.
True Dharma transcends names; thus, it is not a provisional name.
For this reason, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states that all phenomena are free from verbal expression and free from conventional designations (*prajñapti*).
Now, proceeding according to the first gate, it is said that birth and death constitute a conventional designation.
One attains Great Nirvana, seeking liberation that transcends all appellations.
Next is the emergence from afflictions, which consists of four phrases:
first, "emerging from the mud," which teaches the severing of craving.
Craving can defile, being like mud in its nature; to sever and eliminate it is called "emergence.
Second, "absence of attachment" clarifies that because there is no craving, one does not cling to the five sensory objects.
Third, "no-ownership" (*amama*) teaches the removal of views.
Not clinging to self, person, or what belongs to the self is called "no-ownership.
Fourth, "no-appropriation" clarifies that because there are no views, one does not crave false dharmas.
The teaching that issues from the lower [level] concerns karma.
The teachings of various non-Buddhists (tīrthika) that mislead people are called "confusion" (ākulaka); to eliminate and sever these is termed "non-existence" (abhāva).
Such is the meaning of this one principle.
There is another interpretation:
what has been set forth here is divided into four parts.
The first transcends conventional designations and brings about the fruit of liberation from birth and death.
Regarding the phrase "emerging from the mud" (second): this refers to eliminating the causes of affliction (*kleśa*), which consist of views (*dṛṣṭi*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
"Emerging from the mud" at the outset clarifies the elimination of craving;
"being without attachment," and so forth, clarifies the severance of views.
"Speaking of being without attachment" clarifies the severing of the view of self;
"having no 'mine'" means being free from the view of what belongs to a self.
This constitutes the first pair.
Third, being without that which is received, one gives birth to the fruit of transcendence from birth and death;
because one is entirely detached from the five paths of existence, there is nothing to be received.
Fourth, being without agitation or confusion, one clearly severs the causes of karma.
This constitutes another pair:
the former clarifies that which is produced, while the latter clarifies that which is practiced.
Internally rejoicing in and protecting others, one practices the conduct of benefiting others.
To have no jealousy or envy regarding what others do is called "internal destruction of joy.
To comply with them through body and speech is called "protecting their intentions.
"Following meditative concentration" refers to practicing for one's own benefit.
Having few desires and being content, as well as guarding the sense faculties and so forth, can give rise to meditative concentration; therefore, these are called "conformities.
The following clarifies what is to be abandoned:
the complete severance of all evils is termed "being free from all faults."
The above constitutes the distinct teaching (*bhedavyavasthāna*).
"If one can act thus, this is true renunciation" concludes with a praise that reveals its excellence, intended to lead others to practice it.
The above is the second section, clarifying the words of admonition.
From here on, the third section clarifies the benefits of the teaching.
It consists of four distinct parts:
first, Vimalakīrti exhorts the elder and his eldest son that they should both leave the household life; this includes both the initial exhortation and the subsequent explanation.
2. The parents of the elder’s son decline on his behalf.
3. Vimalakīrti instructs him to bring forth his mind; he says that generating the bodhicitta is itself called "leaving home" (pravrajyā) and is itself called "full ordination" (upasampadā).
To seek reality through the characteristics of the breath is called "arousing the mind.
Because of arousing this mind, one abandons all that is evil; being free from the evils of a śrāmaṇera is termed "leaving home immediately."
It also severs all faults of the great bhikṣus and is thus called "fully endowed.
The meaning of the bodhicitta is as extensive as discussed in a separate chapter; this should be explained in full detail.
Fourth, the son of the elder generates the aspiration according to the instruction.
This consists of: first, the departure; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion beginning with "Therefore, I...
Next, [the Buddha] instructs Ānanda to go and inquire after his illness.
The preceding nine individuals clarify their causal practices; the following section, addressed to Ānanda, reveals the Buddha’s fruit-stage virtues.
Ānanda was the Buddha’s younger cousin, and his name means "Joy."
There are three meanings of "joy" (*prīti*), as explained extensively above.
Because he was foremost among the Buddha’s disciples in erudition, the Buddha now addresses him.
First comes the address; afterwards, the refusal.
In this passage, the opening provides a general summary; the section beginning with "The reason why" offers an explanation; and the section beginning with "Therefore" provides a conclusion.
Within the explanation, the phrase "The reason why" serves to inquire about what precedes it and introduce what follows.
The following section provides a detailed analysis, which consists of five distinct parts:
first, citing the circumstances that led to his being rebuked in the past;
second, from the words "Stop, stop" onwards, clarifying the words of the reprimand.
3. From "At that time, O World-Honored One, I was truly filled with shame" onwards, [the text] reveals his own deficiencies;
4. From "Then I heard" onwards, it clarifies how an empty voice arose to harmonize the two houses;
5. From "The wisdom and eloquence of the World-Honored One Vimalakīrti" onwards, it concludes by praising Vimalakīrti and clarifying that he himself could not equal him.
The opening section, "Recalling the Past," refers to the time he was rebuked.
The passage beginning with "World-Honored One" cites the specific incident of the rebuke.
This incident consists of three points:
I. It is explained that the Buddha was ill, and [the narrator] himself went to beg for milk;
II. Vimalakīrti’s inquiry;
III. Ānanda’s reply.
The meaning of the text is entirely clear.
From here on follows the second section, Vimalakīrti’s reprimand.
Why was this necessary?

It was in order to cause Ānanda and all the people of the world to know that the Buddha is eternal, blissful, unconditioned, and free from affliction, so as to cease their false slanders and inspire them toward love and seeking, that it was necessary to instruct and reprove him.
Within this, there are four parts:
first, rebuking him to stop;
second, from "go silently" onwards, driving him away.
3. "Go! and below: he rebukes him and urges him to depart quickly;
4. "You may [go] secretly" and below: he instructs him to depart in secret.
Within the first section, there is first a reprimand and subsequently an instruction.
"Stop, stop, Ānanda; do not speak such words"—this is a word of reprimand.
"The Tathāgata," and so forth, is the instruction.
"The body of the Tathāgata is a vajra-body" clarifies that the Buddha’s essence is firm.
Its substance is firm and difficult to destroy; its nature is identical to that of vajra.
“All evils have been severed and all virtues universally assembled” manifests the Buddha’s perfection of merit.
That “all evils have been severed” signifies the fulfillment of the virtue of cessation.
"The assembly of all virtues and the perfection of practiced conduct" clarify what [the Buddha] possesses;
"What illness could there be? What affliction could there be? manifest what he lacks.
What illness could there be?
There is no internal suffering or illness.
What affliction could there be?
There is no external decay or loss.
This concludes the first section.
From here on, the second section drives them away.
Within this, there are three parts:
first, sending him away in silence;
second, rebuking and admonishing him, forbidding him from slandering the Buddha.
Third, regarding the correct instruction:
"Go silently, Ānanda" was the first dispatch.
He was to cease verbal speech; therefore, he had to go in silence.
"Since I am far away from the place where I beg for alms, I must go there.
The section beginning with "Do not slander" is the second reprimand.
"Do not slander the Tathāgata" serves to restrain what he says.
The Buddha is truly without illness; to claim he is ill and thus misrepresent the Buddha is called slander.
Such slander harms oneself, and for this reason it must be prohibited.
The phrase "Do not let there be differences," etc., serves to halt what has been transmitted.
Because spreading slander harms others, it must also be ceased.
People may be either upright or depraved; when the depraved hear such defamation, they are thereby warned against it.
It is called "coarse" because one must not allow others to hear these crude words that speak of malice and slander.
Even while listening correctly, one must exercise restraint; therefore, it is said: "Do not let the great powerful devas or bodhisattvas from other directions hear these words.
The section beginning with "the Wheel-turning Sage" constitutes the third segment, which instructs by means of principle and teaching.
“The Wheel-Turning Sage King, by virtue of even slight merit, still attains freedom from illness”—this cites the inferior to illustrate the superior.
“How much more so for the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merit,” and so forth—this distinguishes the superior as surpassing the inferior.
This concludes the second section; from here below begins the third, urging [the practitioner] to depart quickly.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, urging the body to depart quickly;...
2. To silence his speech:
"Go, Ānanda," is the first section.
To depart quickly from this place is called "going."
The phrase "Do not let me" and what follows constitutes the latter section, which serves to restrain verbal expression.
"Do not let us suffer this shame" is a general prohibition that cites the transgression.
The Buddha is our teacher, revered by the entire world.
When he speaks of the admonitions for others' illnesses, both sides feel shame; therefore, it is said, "Do not let us suffer disgrace.
The passage beginning with "The non-Buddhist Brahmans" below distinguishes their faults and provides specific prohibitions.
The non-Buddhist brahmins are those who raise objections and slander.
Those who establish principles apart from the Buddha-dharma are called "non-Buddhists" (tīrthika).
Those who bind their intentions to seek purity are described as "brahmins" (brāhmaṇa).
"If one hears these words" clarifies the cause of the slander.
Hearing these words spoken by Ānanda regarding his illness, "one should form this thought: 'What is it to be called a teacher? clarifies the mind of contemptuous slander.
"Being unable to save oneself from illness, yet being able to save others from illness" clarifies the words of light slander.
This concludes the third section; hereafter begins the fourth, which commands him to depart in secret.
Within this, there are three points:
first, one should admonish oneself to depart secretly and swiftly.
If one is not secret, others will see; if one is not swift, others will know. For these reasons, one must depart quickly.
Second, silence their speech so that no one hears it.
Third, enlighten their minds by instructing them correctly through principle.
Within this instruction, first clarify what is correct; from the words "it is not a matter of thought or desire" onwards, reveal what is incorrect.
Regarding the phrase "such a body" and below, this concludes the distinction between what is identical and what is different.
Within this context, the statement "the bodies of all Tathāgatas are the Dharma-body" is a general citation used to illustrate the category.
It clarifies that the Buddha’s response body (*nirmāṇakāya*) is itself the true merit of the *dharmakāya*, and is moreover the body of true *dharmatā*.
This is explained in detail in the "Vajra Body Chapter" of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and in the following section, the "Chapter on Seeing Akṣobhya."
Regarding what is not among the "non-": "the body that is not produced by volition or desire" refers to being free from the cause of fragmented existence (*pariccheda*).
"The Buddha, as World-Honored One, transcends the three realms" refers to being free from the fruit of fragmented existence.

"The Buddha's body is without outflows (*anāsrava*) and all outflows have been exhausted" means that it is free from the cause of transformation and rebirth (*pariṇāma-vaśitā*); as for those outflows that are not yet exhausted, the Buddha has completely eliminated them within the stage of ignorance (*avidyā-bhūmi*).

"The Buddha-body is unconditioned and does not conform to numerical categories": it is free from the fruit of transformation, does not fall into the category of conditioned arising and ceasing, and furthermore, it does not fall into the category of sentient beings.
It is not as you say. To ask, "What illness could this body possibly have? is to confuse what is different with what is not.
This Dharma-body, extending even to the unconditioned, does not fall within the category of numerical bodies; it is forever free from all afflictions—what illness could it possibly have?
The above was the second section, clarifying the wording of the teaching.
From here on is the third section, in which Ānanda addresses the Buddha to confess his own deficiencies:

"At that time, O World-Honored One, I truly felt ashamed," and so forth. The sequence of the text is inverted; it should properly read: "O World-Honored One, at that time I truly felt shame and disgrace, lest I have heard [the Dharma] erroneously."
"At that time" refers to the time when the Way was originally subject to censure.
"I" refers to Ānanda, identifying himself.
"Speaking of the World-Honored One" means reporting the facts to the Buddha.
"Truly harboring shame," etc., means he himself declares his own mind to truly harbor shame and disgrace;
he feels ashamed of what he has said, namely the previous statement that he was ill and required milk.
"Could it be otherwise? and so forth, expresses his doubt regarding what he has heard.
As Vimalakīrti said, the Buddha is truly without illness;
yet, if he requires milk when ill, could this not be my own error in mishearing the Buddha?
From here on, in the fourth section, a voice issues from the sky to harmonize the two parties.
The phrase "immediately a voice from the void was heard" serves as a general heading.
From whom did it issue?
It may have been the Buddha, or Vimalakīrti, or perhaps another powerful deity or celestial being who uttered it.
The following section provides a specific clarification.
The phrase "As the householder said" confirms Vimalakīrti’s words, clarifying that the Buddha’s true body (*dharmakāya*) is indeed free from illness.
The passage beginning with "But for the sake of the Buddha" recounts Ānanda’s words, clarifying that the Buddha’s requirement for milk due to his physical ailment was not in vain.

"However, it is precisely because a Buddha appears in the five turbidities that he manifests this Dharma to deliver sentient beings. This clarifies that Ānanda’s previous mishearing was not an error, as he has now heard correctly.

This statement is inverted; it should properly be said that it is only because the Buddha appears in the world of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) that he manifests this dharma to deliver sentient beings.
Regarding the "five turbidities," as explained in the sūtras:

the first is the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*), wherein the retribution of life is brief, such as the fact that the maximum lifespan for people in the present age is one hundred years, and so forth.
Second is the defilement of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), wherein no virtuous persons exist.
Third is the defilement of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*), wherein greed, hatred, delusion, and other fetters increase.
Fourth is the defilement of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*), wherein false views blaze fiercely.
The fifth is the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*), which refers to famine, pestilence, and warfare.
These five flourishing times are called an evil age, and it is during such a time that a Buddha appears in the world.
Regarding those who manifest this dharma to deliver sentient beings: they manifest the practice of having illness and begging for alms in order to deliver sentient beings.
The matter is as explained in the sutra:
When the Buddha was in the world, there was a brahmin in the city of Vaiśālī who held wrong views and lacked faith.
The Brahmin had a milch cow that was so fierce it surpassed any other in its ferocity, such that no one dared to approach it.
For the sake of delivering this Brahmin, the Buddha indicated that he had fallen ill and required milk for his treatment.
Ānanda went to beg for the Buddha, carrying his alms bowl as he approached the man's gate.
Upon seeing him, the brāhmaṇa became angry and asked,
"What do you require?"
Ānanda replied, “The Buddha is ill and requires milk; that is why he has come to beg for it.
Upon hearing this, he thought to himself:
"You may take it yourself; let the ox leap over and kill you.
He then said to Ānanda, "If you need some, you may milk it."
Ānanda said, “Very well.
He immediately went to where the cow was; the cow opened its legs of her own accord, allowing him to milk it.
The cow said to Ānanda, "I pray that you leave one portion of milk to beg for my calf; all the rest I offer to the Buddha.
The calf then spoke:
"I offer everything to the Tathāgata; I shall eat grass and water.
A Brahmin standing nearby witnessed this entirely and immediately reproached himself:
"I am not equal to this ox; I failed to recognize a field of merit and gave rise to such an evil thought."
Consequently, he developed deep reverence and faith toward the Buddha;
thus it is said that he was manifesting the practice of liberating sentient beings.
Regarding the instruction, "Ānanda, take the milk without feeling shame," this was spoken to Ānanda—who had previously felt genuine shame—to encourage him not to feel ashamed.
Because he was exhorted to go begging, he therefore went to beg;
because he was exhorted to accept milk, he therefore took the milk.
Since going on alms-round for the sake of transformation is what is appropriate for a sage, he was exhorted not to feel ashamed.
This concludes the fourth section.
"The wisdom and eloquence of the World-Honored One Vimalakīrti are such as this" constitutes the fifth section, which summarizes and praises Vimalakīrti.
The preceding part provides the statement, the subsequent part offers the explanation, and the section beginning with "Therefore" provides the conclusion.
The preceding section consists of the individual inquiries regarding the illness addressed to ten people.
The passage beginning with "Thus, the five hundred great disciples... collectively mentions the remaining individuals.
At that time, the Tathāgata addressed each one individually; as it would be impossible to list them all exhaustively, the compilers have summarized and mentioned them collectively.

Chapter 4: On the Bodhisattvas (Part 2, End). Regarding the "Chapter on the Bodhisattvas": In the preceding chapter, the Śrāvakas were summoned to inquire after [the Buddha’s] illness; they declined, citing their incapacity. Now, the Bodhisattvas are summoned.
Accordingly, the title of this chapter is set as "The Chapter on the Bodhisattvas.
There are briefly three reasons for its inclusion:

first, in the preceding chapter, the Śrāvakas were commanded to inquire after the illness [of the Buddha], but they declined, stating they were incapable; it was therefore necessary to command the Bodhisattvas, and thus this chapter follows.
The second reason this chapter appears is to manifest that Vimalakīrti’s virtue is sublime.
What does this mean?
In the preceding chapter, the Śrāvakas were summoned to inquire after his illness, thereby demonstrating that Vimalakīrti’s virtue surpasses that of the Two Vehicles.
This chapter addresses the Bodhisattva Āyuṣmat as he inquires after [Vimalakīrti’s] illness, in order to manifest that Vimalakīrti excels all other bodhisattvas;
it appears here for the third purpose of revealing what Vimalakīrti has taught.
What is the meaning of this?
In the preceding "Chapter on Expedient Means," because the inquiry into illness was initiated by ordinary people, it extensively elucidates Vimalakīrti’s teaching of the Dharma for ordinary people;
in the aforementioned "Chapter on the Disciples," because he addressed the śrāvakas, it extensively elucidates Vimalakīrti’s teaching of the Dharma for the śrāvakas.
In this present chapter, because it addresses the bodhisattvas and further elucidates the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas taught by Vimalakīrti, its title reveals what is being expounded.

Within the subsequent section that clarifies the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas, the meaning has both specific and general applications. Specifically, this chapter clarifies the instruction of bodhisattvas; generally, however, everything from here through the subsequent "Chapter on the Buddha of Fragrant Accumulation" constitutes the Dharma for instructing bodhisattvas within this assembly.

Regarding this general discussion, first we shall examine this chapter in relation to the subsequent text to distinguish its similarities and differences; next, we shall provide a general outline; and finally, we shall offer a detailed explanation.
As for what these similarities and differences are:
There are five kinds of distinctions.
First, regarding the meaning: in this present chapter, by contrasting [Vimalakīrti] with those who are incapable, his noble and exalted human virtues are manifested;
in the following "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter, by contrasting him with those who are capable, the subtlety of his virtues is revealed.
Regarding the second meaning: in this present chapter, the text extensively elucidates Vimalakīrti’s invincible eloquence to demonstrate the excellence of his wisdom;
in the subsequent "Chapter on Inquiring after His Illness," it extensively elucidates Vimalakīrti’s mastery of spiritual transformations to manifest the excellence of his supernormal powers.

Regarding the third meaning: in this present chapter, the virtues of Vimalakīrti’s liberation are extensively revealed by means of the words of others; in the following "Chapter on Inquiring after His Illness," Vimalakīrti himself reveals the virtues of his liberation.
Regarding the fourth meaning: within this chapter, because [the Buddha] addressed those who were incapable, he extensively revealed the Dharma previously taught by Vimalakīrti;

from the "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter (*Vyādhikathana-parivarta*) onwards, because he addressed those who were capable of going there to inquire after his illness, he clarified what is being taught now.

Regarding the fifth meaning: in this chapter below, the essence of the dharmas practiced by bodhisattvas is elucidated; in the "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter below, the characteristics of the cultivation and accomplishment thereof are elucidated.
Such are the differences in characteristics.
As for what is called "sameness," there are three kinds:
first, sameness in teaching; this chapter shares the same teaching as the subsequent [section on] Bodhisattvas.
Second, the identity of the Dharma: both are taught through the very same dharmas practiced by bodhisattvas.
Third, the distinction of the identity of practice: within this chapter, the analysis of practice is twofold, namely realization and teaching.
In the beginning, facing Maitreya, his realized practice (*adhigama-caryā*) is clarified—namely, teaching the devaputra to abandon signs and realize the truth;
subsequently, facing other persons, his teaching practice (*deśanā-caryā*) is clarified.
The "Inquiry into the Illness" chapter (*Vyākaraṇa-parivarta*) also distinguishes these two.
The *Introduction to the Gate of Non-duality* clarifies the practice of realization (*adhigama-pratipatti*), while the remainder clarifies the practice of teaching (*deśanā-pratipatti*).
Such are their similarities and differences.
Next follows the general structural analysis.
Regarding the section on "Teaching the Bodhisattva Dharma," there are two broad divisions and four detailed subdivisions. As for the two broad divisions:
from this point until the end of the "Entrance into the Non-dual Gate" chapter, it elucidates the cause and effect of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma-body;
from the "Incense Accumulation" chapter onward, it elucidates the cause and effect of the Bodhisattva’s Pure Land.
As for the fourfold subdivision: first, in contrast with Maitreya, it clarifies the fruit of the Dharmakāya; the true nature of bodhi is its fruit.
From the section "First Adorning" [of the *Avatamsaka Sūtra*] down to the end of the "Gate of Non-duality," it clarifies the causes of the Dharmakāya.
At the beginning of the "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation," it clarifies the fruit of the Pure Land.
The end of the "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation" clarifies the causes for the Pure Land; practicing the ten [perfections] or the eight [liberations] is precisely what is meant here.
The general outline is thus.
Next, there follows a detailed explanation.

In this chapter, many individuals are addressed; the first four are listed individually, while the phrase "in this manner, each of these bodhisattvas [addressed] the others" and so forth summarizes the remainder.
Within the preceding section on distinctions, he first addresses Maitreya to clarify the fruit of the Dharmakāya.
"Maitreya" is his clan name; this translates as "Compassion. His given name is Ajita, which means "Unconquerable. He was the son of a high minister in Vārāṇasī.

When Maitreya was first born, he was endowed with all the primary and secondary marks of excellence. King Brahmadatta of Vārāṇasī, having heard that his auspicious marks surpassed those of ordinary men, feared he would become a threat to the kingdom and intended to cause him harm; he therefore requested him from his father to keep him under his own care.
The father, knowing the king’s intention, replied to him,
“I shall take her to my own family.
Upon returning home, he immediately dispatched people to send her to the foreign family in the kingdom of Pāpālika in South India to be raised by them.

Maitreya’s maternal uncle was surnamed Pāpali; his hair was deep blue-black, he possessed the physical mark of hands reaching his knees, and being wise and profoundly learned, he served as a leader among the teachers of the world, instructing others according to what he himself knew.
Maitreya followed him at the age of seven to receive instruction; what he mastered in a single day exceeded the learning of many years, and before long, he had exhausted [the teacher's] knowledge.
His maternal uncle, wishing to manifest Maitreya’s virtue, intended to hold an unrestricted great assembly (anāvaraṇa-mahāpariṣad) at his own home to display it.
Having few goods in their own home, they sent two disciples to Maitreya’s house to fetch wealth and property.

On the way, the two disciples heard that the Buddha had just appeared in the world; they turned back to see him, and at that moment, both were devoured by a tiger. Because they had directed their minds toward the Buddha, they were reborn together in the heavens, and thus the mission was never fulfilled.
Having waited for a long time without success, Pāpali led all his household members to prepare a sacrificial feast.

When the seven days of the festival had concluded, a certain brahmin arrived last; finding that both wealth and food were exhausted and he had obtained nothing at all, he became greatly incensed and said to Pāpali:
"I shall surely use a divine spell to shatter your head into seven pieces!"
When Pāpali heard this, he was overcome with extreme grief and distress.
His two former disciples, who had been reborn in the heavens, saw their teacher grieving from afar and asked him from mid-air:
"Teacher, why are you so distressed?"
Then Pāpali fully explained his reasons in response to the two devas,
and they immediately asked him:
"Who are these devas that have come to question you?"
The deva answered him fully and said to him:
"A Buddha has already appeared in the world; why do you not go to see him?
What is the use of grieving in vain?"

Pāpāli had previously read prophetic scriptures and knew that a Buddha was appearing; hearing what had been announced, he immediately dispatched Maitreya with sixteen others to verify whether it was true or false. He instructed them to observe whether the Buddha’s thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics were complete, and further taught them to ask their question mentally in a secluded place:
"Who is our teacher?"
"How many years old are you now?
And how many marks do you have upon your body?
Maitreya, having received these instructions, went there to verify them.
Seeing that the Buddha’s marks and signs were clearly and fully perfected, he thought of a question in his mind; as soon as he asked it, the Buddha answered him in full.

At that time, Maitreya and sixteen others left the household life to follow the Buddha. Those sixteen people immediately became arhats, but Maitreya alone did not seek the exhaustion of outflows, vowing instead to seek the path of the Buddha.

At that time, the Tathāgata immediately bestowed upon him a prophecy, declaring that after his next rebirth he would ascend to the heavens, and having completed his celestial lifespan, he would descend to Jambudvīpa to attain the path of Buddhahood.
The characteristics of his attainment of the Way are explained in detail as set forth in the sutra.
The Buddha now addresses him, first speaking and then taking leave.

In the farewell, he first clarifies that he himself is incapable [of the task]; the section beginning with "For this reason" provides the explanation; and the section beginning with "Therefore I" concludes it.
In the commentary, the phrase "The reason why" interrogates what precedes to introduce what follows.
Below, this is formally analyzed; within this analysis, there are three parts:
first, citing the circumstances by which [the Buddha] was previously rebuked.
2. From "At that time, Vimalakīrti" onwards, the text reveals the words of Vimalakīrti’s instruction and reprimand.
3. From "World-Honored One, when Vimalakīrti preached this Dharma" onwards, it clarifies the benefits of that instruction and reprimand.
At the beginning, the phrase "Recalling the Past" introduces the occasion of being rebuked;
"preaching the stage of non-retrogression for the King of Tuṣita and his retinue" reveals the specific matter of that rebuke.
Because the Buddha had prophesied that Maitreya would relinquish his body and be reborn in Tuṣita, the King of Tuṣita and his retinue frequently came to request the Dharma.
On one occasion, he came to inquire about the practices of the stages (bhūmi-caryā), and Maitreya explained them for him.

The stages from the "Pure Mind" (śuddhacitta) upward are called the Stage of Non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*); alternatively, those stages above the "Spiritual Lineage" (*gotra*) may also be termed the Stage of Non-retrogression.

The practice that leads toward these stages is called "stage-practice" (*bhūmi-caryā*); alternatively, one may ask whether the practice that accomplishes these stages is what is termed stage-practice.
That deva asked about the meaning of the cultivation and realization of the marks; Maitreya explained it for him, but because his explanation concealed the reality, he was rebuked.
From here begins the second section, where Vimalakīrti instructs and rebukes him.
Why must this be done? It is because one must instruct and reprimand the various devas so that they abandon their meditative cultivation and enter into realization.
"Come and say" is a general reference.

The following provides a detailed explanation. Within this detailed text, there is first a censure and subsequently an instruction. From the beginning up to the phrase "nor is there any falling back" constitutes the words of censure, censuring them so that they may relinquish [their attachments].

The passage from "Maitreya, you should cause these sons of heaven to relinquish their conceptual discrimination" onwards constitutes the words of instruction, instructing them so that they may realize the truth.

Within the preceding section on "Rebuking," the text relies upon Maitreya to refute and dismantle the meaning of attaining enlightenment through the prediction of future attainment (*vyākaraṇa*), thereby clarifying by analogy that all things are ultimately unattainable.
This section contains two parts:
first, the refutation of Maitreya’s meaning regarding the attainment of enlightenment after one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
2. "Therefore, Maitreya, do not use this dharma to entice the devaputra," and so forth, serves as a general conclusion and reprimand.
Within the preceding section, first his attainment is presented; then, from "For what purpose? onwards, it is refuted to reveal its non-existence.
Among those cited, the mention of "Maitreya" is to address that specific individual.
The phrase "The World-Honored One bestows" and so forth cites what has been attained.
"Bestowing upon you the prediction" means that through the cultivation of causes, the fruit is realized.
It is certain that this will not be lost; just as when the mind records an object with firm mindfulness so that it is not forgotten, it is called "recording" (*jì*).
When the Sage records and shows it to others, it is termed "bestowing" (*shòu*).

Regarding the phrase "one more birth": having received the prediction among humans, after casting off this body one is reborn in Tuṣita, and subsequently taking birth again in the human realm, one then attains Buddhahood.
Because there is an interval between that [birth] in Tuṣita and the single retribution [of this life], it is called "one birth" (*ekajāti*). Question:
If one must first be born above in Tuṣita and subsequently be born among humans before finally becoming a Buddha, this constitutes two births; why then do you say "one"?
The commentary states:
"Regarding this birth, the Noble Ones say it is indeterminate.
According to the treatise of Nāgārjuna:

Maitreya considers this to be three lifetimes: the present life, which is not counted because it is merely the final exhaustion of delusion; and the subsequent birth in the human realm, which is likewise not counted because it is already the Buddha-body; thus, for these reasons, he speaks of "one."
Question:

If one who is destined to be born once in the heavens and subsequently born in the human realm to attain Buddhahood is called "one-lifetime" (ekajāti-pratibaddha), then how many of the fourteen births are included in the case of a Srotāpanna who attains nirvāṇa after being born once in the heavens and once in the human realm?
The commentary states:
"Among these fourteen births, they are termed two births.
If that is so, Maitreya should likewise be the same as them; how can it be said that he is one?"
The commentary states:
Although they should be spoken of as equal, they are described as distinct because their respective expectations differ.
Since that *srotāpanna* expects the exhaustion of the body and the remainderless *nirvāṇa*, he undergoes two more bodies, which constitute two births.

For those such as Maitreya, when compared to the Buddha’s body, their subsequent birth in the human realm is itself the Buddha-body; therefore, in relation to that [Buddha] body, the single retribution of the Tuṣita heaven is specifically designated as "one."
Regarding the statement "attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*," there are generally two interpretations:
first, the true (*tathatā*), and second, the responsive (*nirmāṇa*).
That which accords with actual practice is called the true; that which manifests through the eight phases of enlightenment is said to be the responsive.
This [attainment] should be understood as having an indeterminate location for its actual realization. If one discusses the locations where its accomplishment is attained, there are three:
first, attaining bodhi upon entering the stage of the lineage (*gotrabhūmi*). As the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"The *srotāpanna* reaches it after eighty thousand kalpas, and so on up to the *pratyekabuddha*, who reaches it after ten thousand kalpas," thereby reaching the six types of bodhi.
It should be understood that these are called "reaching the lineage" (gotra) as it pertains to attaining bodhi.
Second, entering the first stage (*bhūmi*) is called "attaining bodhi," as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-śāstra*.

Regarding the statement in the "Chapter on the Distinction of Merits" (*Guṇaparikīrtana*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* concerning those who attain bodhi after eight births down to one birth, this refers to attaining the realized wisdom (*adhigama-jñāna*) of the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Third, reaching the end of time is called "attaining bodhi"; the meaning of this can be understood.
Alternatively, it may be divided into five stages as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*:

first, the bodhi of generating the mind (*cittotpāda-bodhi*), which consists of generating the bodhicitta within the immeasurable ocean of birth and death, situated in the realms of fortunate rebirth.
2. Bodhi of Subduing the Mind: deeply subduing afflictions; its stage is above that of the lineage (*gotra*) and within the stage of the patience of subduing (*vinaya-kṣānti*).
3. Bodhi of Illumination: cultivating clear wisdom; its stage is from the first ground (*bhūmi*) upward.

Fourth, emerging and reaching Bodhi: transcending existence and non-existence and arriving at the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), this stage occurs from the seventh bhūmi upward.
Fifth, unsurpassed Bodhi: the ultimate consummation, situated at the fruit of Buddhahood.
If subdivided further, these categories can also be numerous.
Regarding the *Prasaṅgika* system, all capacities exist from the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) upward.
According to the *Avataṃsaka*, even at the stage of the "Worthy One" (*bhadra-mukha*), one is capable of manifesting the eight aspects [of a Buddha's life] without attaining perfect enlightenment.
What is discussed here is the *prasanga* (consequentialist) method; attaining enlightenment is defined as achieving Buddhahood through the eight aspects.
Below follows a refutation of this position, which consists of four distinct sections:
first, a refutation of the existence of attainment by challenging the notion of arising within the context of phenomenal characteristics (*dharmas*).
2. From "If one receives the prediction based on non-arising" onwards, the existence of attainment is refuted by means of the dharma of non-arising that dispels phenomena;

3. From "If one receives the prediction based on arising from suchness" onwards, the existence of attainment is refuted by means of the arising and ceasing of true dharmas within dependent origination;
4. From "All arising is suchness" onwards, the existence of attainment is refuted by means of the meaning of the equality of true nature.
Within these four sections, there is a distinction between what is implicit and what is explicit.

In the first section, the focus is primarily on refuting the attainment of a prediction (*vyākaraṇa*). In the second section, the refutation concerns both the attainment of a prediction and the attainment of enlightenment (*bodhi*). In the third section, the focus is primarily on refuting the difficulty of attaining a prediction. In the fourth section, the refutation concerns both the attainment of a prediction and the attainment of enlightenment.
The first part consists of two sections:
first, challenging and refuting the attainment of the prediction (vyākaraṇa) by means of the arising of the three periods of time;

second, from "As the Buddha has said" onwards, clarifying that arising lacks intrinsic nature by citing the four characteristics (lakṣaṇa) which are simultaneous and identical in essence, thereby establishing that there is no attainment of the prediction.
In the first part of the middle section, the initial statement, "By what kind of birth does one receive the prediction? serves as a general inquiry.
The subsequent statements, "Is it in the past? Is it in the future? and so forth, establish specific determinations according to the time periods.
Because his advance and retreat are uncertain, he speaks thus.
From the words "If [it were] past" onwards, there is a specific refutation according to the world.
If one were to receive a prediction (vyākaraṇa) based on a past birth, since the past has already ceased, upon what could the prediction be based?
If one receives a prediction regarding a future birth, that future birth has not yet arrived;
upon what, then, is the prediction based?
If one receives a prediction regarding the present birth, the present birth does not abide; how, then, can a prediction be received?
Appearing for a moment and then ceasing, it does not abide for even an instant; therefore, it is said to be "non-abiding.
Since arising itself does not abide, who could wait for a prediction and thereby receive one?

The subsequent passage further clarifies that the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are of the same essence as arising, demonstrating that arising lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), thereby establishing that there is no one to receive a prediction.
"According to what the Buddha has said: 'O bhikṣu, you have now been born at this very moment,'" and so forth, citing the Buddha’s former words.
It is said that there are three types of the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*):
first, the four characteristics of before and after.
In a single moment, conditioned phenomena undergo four phases: first arising, next abiding, then changing, and finally ceasing.
These two [sets of characteristics] are simultaneous yet distinct entities—the four marks.

Apart from conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), there exist distinct characteristics of arising that are neither form nor mind, capable of producing all phenomena; likewise, there exists a distinct characteristic of cessation that ceases phenomena.
These three [characteristics] are simultaneous and of the same substance as the four characteristics.
As stated in the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra* and this sutra, what is the meaning of this?
The characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) have no substantial reality; they are like illusions, mirages, water [in a mirage], and so forth.
Within this Dharma, the existence of characteristics is called arising, and their emptiness is called cessation.
The existence of characteristics is called arising, yet arising does not precede cessation;
the emptiness of characteristics is called cessation, yet cessation does not follow arising.
That these illusory phenomena of arising and ceasing are established is called "abiding.
Furthermore, that these illusory phenomena each maintain their own specific characteristics is also called "abiding.
Thus, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* states:
Because it abides by its own nature, it is called "abiding.
This abiding is not something external to arising and ceasing.
Since the meanings and aspects of that arising and ceasing are each distinct, they are called "difference."

Furthermore, that which differs from the nature of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is also called "different," and that which differs from the reality of sensory objects (*viṣaya*) is likewise called "different.
This difference, moreover, is not something external to arising, ceasing, and so forth.

Because the four characteristics are simultaneous and of one essence, the Buddha declared: "O Bhikṣu, at this very moment you are also being born, aging, and ceasing," because they are of one essence.
In terms of the meaning of the remaining three characteristics, they are designated as "arising"; yet apart from those three, there is no separate nature of arising.
Since arising lacks intrinsic nature, arising is itself non-arising; who, then, could be granted a prediction [of enlightenment]?
Even when speaking of cessation in terms of the other three characteristics, cessation has no distinct nature.
Because cessation lacks intrinsic nature, cessation is itself non-cessation; who, then, could be said to receive a prediction?
Therefore, ultimately, there is no one who receives a prediction.
From here on, the second section refutes the attainment of bodhi through the difficulty of non-arising (*anutpāda*).
Why is this necessary?
It is because one fears that Maitreya, being born in a state of non-existence (*abhāva*), might falsely establish the meaning of attaining existence; therefore, he subjects it to this refutation.
Regarding the statement, "If one receives the prediction [of enlightenment] through non-arising," this is to take up what was previously established by way of contradiction.
When the Way says, "Non-arising is the true state (samyaktva-niyāma)," it establishes its underlying principle.
What is meant is that this is the true position of the Sovereign (Bhūtatathatā), not the position of practice.
It is similar to what is said regarding abiding in the center: "This dharma abides in the station of dharmas.
Within this true position, there is neither the attainment of a prediction nor the attainment of bodhi; this is because, according to principle, attainment is negated.
"How is it that Maitreya receives the prediction of one more birth? This is a critique based on the principle of the Dharma.
From here below, the third section refutes the attainment of the prediction by examining the arising and ceasing of true dharmas within dependent origination.
The true dharma-body is uniformly termed "Suchness" (*tathatā*).

Following deluded sentiments, it manifests as arising and ceasing; following deluded thoughts, it gives rise to defilement, which is termed "arising," while its purity being obscured is termed "ceasing."
Furthermore, according to the purification that arises as an antidote, it is called "arising"; according to the cessation of defilement, it is called "extinction.
The arising of dependent origination is not arising as arising; arising is non-arising.
The extinction of dependent origination is not extinction as extinction; extinction is non-extinction.
It is like a person who, in the darkness of night, sees a rope and takes it for a snake. The thought "snake" arises; yet that which arises is without arising.
When morning comes and the illusion of the snake vanishes, that which vanishes is without vanishing.
Since both arising and vanishing are non-existent, upon what basis can one speak of "attainment"?
In the text, two positions regarding arising and ceasing are first established: "arising from Suchness" is the first position;
"ceasing from Suchness" is the second position.
Because they receive the Buddha’s prediction based on the nature of arising and ceasing, they are said to be "from" [the path].
Because their progress and retreat are not fixed, they are both termed "heretical" (*ya*).
Below, this is challenged.
"If one were to receive the prediction based on the suchness of arising," this refers back to what was previously established;
it is refuted by reasoning that suchness has no arising.
"If one were to receive the prediction based on the suchness of cessation," this restates what was subsequently established.
Just as there is no cessation, it cannot be refuted by logical argument.
Since it is neither arising nor ceasing—non-arising being treated as arising, yet when there is arising, there is no arising;
non-ceasing being treated as ceasing, yet when there is ceasing, there is no ceasing—it is therefore said to be "non-existent."
Since arising and ceasing are both non-existent, upon what basis could a prediction be granted?
From here on, the fourth section refutes the notion of partial attainment by means of the principle of the equality of true nature.
True nature is a single suchness; ordinary beings and sages are equal.
Since there is nothing to be attained within suchness (*tathatā*), how could Maitreya alone have an attainment within suchness?
The text contains three sections:
the first section refutes the attainment of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), while the latter two sections refute the attainment of the fruit (*phala*).

Within the section on the difficulty of attaining prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), it first clarifies that both ordinary beings and sages are all suchness (*tathatā*); next, it refutes partial attainment. The section beginning with "Therefore" provides the explanation.
The preceding statement, "All sentient beings are suchness," refers to the suchness of ordinary people.

As for "the suchness of sentient beings," it refers to how sentient beings are formed through the integration of the nature of phenomena and dependent origination; because their characteristics are subsumed back into the fundamental source, sentient beings are suchness.
Regarding "the suchness of dharmas," this generally clarifies that both mundane and sagely dharmas are suchness.
Just as all phenomena are integrated through the dependent origination of suchness (*tathatā*), and because they are subsumed from their very source, suchness itself is also "as-it-is" (*yathā*).
Regarding the phrase "the suchness of the various sages up to Maitreya," this refers to the suchness of the sages.
Just as the nature of dependent origination integrates all the noble ones, and because they are subsumed within that fundamental source, all sages are identical to Suchness (*tathatā*).
It is like water forming waves—the waves are nothing but water;
or like gold being fashioned into vessels—the vessels are still gold. These cases are likewise so.
Next, the objection is raised:
"If Maitreya has received the prediction," this cites what he has attained;
"then all sentient beings should also receive the prediction," this uses ordinary beings as a point of inquiry.
The following explains the intent of the objection.
"So why" (*so yi*) is an interrogative particle. It asks:
for what reason do I say that "Maitreya attains [it], and sentient beings also attain it"?
The following provides an explanation of this:
it is because the meaning of "suchness" (tathatā) is neither dual nor differentiated.
Since suchness has no "this" or "that," it is called non-dual; since suchness has no superiority or inferiority, it is said to be non-differentiated.
Since they are not different, if one receives a prediction of enlightenment within the suchness of Maitreya, one should likewise receive that prediction within the suchness of sentient beings.
If no one receives a prediction within the suchness of sentient beings, what is there to be obtained within the suchness of Maitreya?

In the refutation below, which achieves the realization of the fruit, there is first a refutation of the meaning of attaining *bodhi*, followed by a refutation of the meaning of Maitreya attaining *nirvāṇa*.
Within the former, the phrase "Maitreya attains *bodhi*" cites that which he has established.
"All sentient beings should likewise attain it" uses the category of ordinary beings as a point of inquiry.
The following explains the intent of this objection.
"So why? is the interrogative phrase used to raise the question.
Why do I say that Maitreya “attains birth and also attains it”?
The following passage explains this:
all sentient beings are the very mark of bodhi; since they are identical to Maitreya, Maitreya attains sentient beings and also attains them.
The essence and characteristics of bodhi are as explained in the following passage: "Quiescence is bodhi, because all marks have been extinguished.
Non-contemplation is bodhi, because it is free from all conditions."
"Non-practice is bodhi, because it is free from recollection.
Thus, this nature of bodhi is a collection formed through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
It collects the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) of sentient beings; by grasping conditions according to reality, all arising is itself bodhi.
The true nature of Maitreya is itself bodhi; since Maitreya has attainment, the true nature of sentient beings is also bodhi, and they too should have attainment.
Yet, the true nature of sentient beings is itself bodhi, and within this bodhi there is no mark of a sentient being, nor is there any attainment of a sentient being.
The true nature of Maitreya is itself bodhi; within this bodhi, where could there be [a self] such that one could say, "Maitreya is able to attain" it?
The following section refutes the notion that Maitreya attains nirvāṇa.
The statement, "If Maitreya were to attain parinirvāṇa," cites what he has attained.
The phrase, "All sentient beings would likewise attain parinirvāṇa," uses ordinary beings as a point of comparison.
"Nirvāṇa" (nièdù) is what is called by foreigners;
the following explains the intent of the objection.
"So why" (*suo yǐ*) is a rhetorical inquiry.
Regarding my question, "How is it that Maitreya attains the extinction of sentient beings?
the following passage provides the explanation.

The Buddha knows that sentient beings are ultimately quiescent; they possess the very mark of *nirvāṇa* and do not need to be extinguished further. Since he is identical to Maitreya in this regard, Maitreya attains the extinction of sentient beings as well.
The essential nature and characteristics of *nirvāṇa* are as explained above.
That which was originally unarisen is likewise unextinguished; this is the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, it is as stated in that *Bhūmi-sūtra*:
The essential nature is eternally quiescent, neither ceasing nor arising; this is the meaning of *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, as it is said in that *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
"Great Parinirvāṇa has existed inherently from the beginning; it is not something that has come into being only now."
It is neither real nor unreal, neither born nor created, neither one nor different, neither past, future, nor present, and neither cause nor effect.
This is precisely what is called the single Truth of the Cessation of Suffering in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
The Sūtra itself explains:
"It is not because it destroys phenomena that it is called the cessation of suffering (*duḥkhanirodha*).

What is called the cessation of suffering is that which is beginningless and unconditioned, without arising and without exhaustion, eternally abiding beyond exhaustion, naturally pure, and free from all afflictions—this is its cessation of suffering."
This nature of nirvāṇa is that which, through dependent origination, constitutes the sentient beings of saṃsāra;
when its marks are extinguished, it is the reality itself, and thus all birth is the very mark of nirvāṇa.
This is its essential characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), not a conventional sign (*nimitta*).
Within this *dharmatā-nirvāṇa*, there has never been any characteristic of a sentient being that could be extinguished; therefore, it is said that it is no longer subject to extinction.
That there is no birth to be extinguished is the ultimate extinction; therefore, it is called "ultimate" (atyanta).
This principle is eternally fixed and is realized only by a Buddha; thus, it is said that the Buddha knows it.
This nature of nirvana is identical in principle for both sentient beings and Maitreya.
Since cessation is no different [in both cases], if Maitreya has attainment, sentient beings must likewise have attainment.

Yet, within this *dharmatā-nirvāṇa*, there is ultimately no birth that attains nirvāṇa; since Maitreya is identical to this, how could he alone be said to have attainment? Why do you speak of his attainment in such a biased manner?

Question: Nirvana is the meritorious fruit of Buddhahood; it exists only upon reaching that fruit. How, then, can it be proclaimed that all sentient beings are already in nirvana? There are three ways to explain this meaning: 1. The nature of nirvana is the true reality (*dharmatā*). Since the nature of all phenomena is originally quiescent, it is said that all sentient beings are already in nirvana. 2. The nature of nirvana is the absence of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Since the nature of all phenomena is originally free from conceptual proliferation, it is said that all sentient beings are already in nirvana. 3. The nature of nirvana is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Since the nature of all phenomena is originally the ultimate truth, it is said that all sentient beings are already in nirvana.
First, regarding the explanation of conditions (*pratyaya*):
having severed birth and death, one separately attains *nirvāṇa*; therefore, the sūtras proclaim *nirvāṇa* as mutual non-existence.
Second, discussing reality in terms of conditions.
By transforming the substance of birth and death into nirvāṇa, it is said that nirvāṇa is the fruit of the cause of realization.
Third, regarding reality as it truly is:
the substance of birth and death is itself nirvāṇa; it does not depend upon any transition or transformation.

For example, in the darkness of night one may see a rope and mistake it for a snake; yet when one with clear vision examines it, the snake is seen to be nothing but the rope—how could there be any need for transformation?
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The Great Parinirvāṇa is inherently present from the very beginning."
Furthermore, the treatise also states:
"The intrinsic nature is eternally quiescent; it is not that there was defilement previously which is later abandoned.
The meaning of what is discussed here corresponds to the latter point.
Furthermore, speaking in terms of persons, there are ordinary beings and sages; yet ordinary beings and sages are of one essence.

From the perspective of the ordinary being looking toward the sage, the sage is obscured by delusions; however, when that same essence later manifests as pure virtue, it serves as the fundamental basis for what is called "Buddha-nature" and "Nirvana-nature. At that stage, it is not yet termed "Buddha," nor is it termed "Nirvana."

According to the Buddha’s perspective, the essence of those sentient beings has been eternally pure from the beginning; it is free from the concealment of delusion and need not be further extinguished, and for this reason, it is primordial nirvana itself.
What is discussed here is based on the perspective of the Buddha; therefore, it is said that the Buddha’s knowledge is itself nirvāṇa.
The preceding section was the first, which extensively refuted the existence of attainment.
From here on is the second section, which concludes with a general reprimand.
Regarding the statement, "Therefore, Maitreya, do not use this dharma to entice the devaputras," this refers back to the previous direct rebuke.
Because Maitreya previously had nothing to be attained, he has no dharma acquired through cultivation according to signs with which to entice the devaputras.
"Truly, there is neither one who sets forth nor one who retreats"—this is a reprimand based on the analysis of principle.
Since, according to principle, there is no person, there is "no one who sets forth.
"Nor is there anyone who retreats"—with this, the preceding reprimand is concluded.
"I shall instruct them next.
"Maitreya, you should cause these sons of heaven to abandon their conceptual views regarding bodhi," he said, exhorting them in general.
The section beginning with "The reason why" provides the explanation.
First, an objection is raised:
"Enlightenment is excellent; for what reason must it be abandoned?
Below, this is answered and explained.
Within this, one should first explain the meaning of *bodhi*, and subsequently explain the text; the meaning is treated in a separate chapter.
At the beginning of the text, the statement that "bodhi cannot be attained by body or mind" briefly opens two gates.
"Quiescence" (*śānti*) concludes the preceding section on the broad exposition; "Incomparable" (*anupama*) concludes the subsequent section.
Within the opening of the previous section, it was asked: why can [Bodhi] not be attained by body or mind?

Because the true nature of Bodhi is wondrously quiescent and free from marks, it cannot be attained by the body as it is beyond the reach of the five sensory faculties; it cannot be attained by the mind as it is beyond the reach of mental objects.
Furthermore, that which possesses a body is not bodhi; only that which is bodiless is it. Therefore, it cannot be attained by means of a body.
That which possesses a mind is not it; only that which is mindless is it. Therefore, it cannot be attained by means of a mind.
Question: The sutras state that the Buddha attained bodhi; how can it be said that it is unattainable?
Explanation:
Regarding the conventional enumeration of words, it is said that the Buddha attained [enlightenment]; yet in reality, at the time of attainment, there is no one who attains.
Why is this so? Apart from bodhi, there is no self or person; who then can be said to attain it?
Since both the self and persons do not exist, there is likewise no enlightenment outside of persons that can be realized; thus, there is nothing to be attained.

When one does not perceive the self or persons as distinct from enlightenment, only then is it called reaching the ultimate limit of enlightenment, and for this reason, it is further termed "attainment."
Since the self and persons are thus, the body and mind are likewise.
Apart from bodhi, there is no separate body or mind; therefore, there is nothing that can attain it.
Since body and mind do not exist, there is also nothing apart from these two—body and mind—that constitutes a bodhi which could be cultivated or realized; therefore, there is nothing to be attained.
When one does not perceive the body and mind as distinct from the time of awakening, only then is it called reaching the ultimate, true awakening;
thus, it is also termed "attainment. This is because one cannot establish either body or mind [as real]; therefore, one must relinquish the view of attaining awakening.
Next, this is explained in detail.
Within this, first it clarifies that [the Dharma] cannot be attained by the mind.
From the phrase "does not meet" (*bùhuì*) onwards, it extensively reveals the meaning of its inability to be attained by the body.

In the preceding clarification that the mind cannot be apprehended, there are fourteen phrases. Of these, the first thirteen—whose essence is quiescent and free from characteristics—constitute one's own virtue; the final phrase, whose function of wisdom is clear and lucid, constitutes the benefit of others.

Within the first thirteen [points], the initial ten clarify the departure from the characteristics of the cognizing mind (*ālambaka-citta*), while the latter three clarify the departure from the characteristics of the cognized phenomena (*ālambana-dharma*).
Among the first ten statements, the initial seven concern the departure from characteristics, while the final three concern reality itself.

In the preceding section on the "Separation from Characteristics," the first sentence serves as the general statement; the next two clarify the establishment of the two [aspects], which in turn serve as the basis;
and the final four explain and establish them. Within the initial general statement, "Nirvana is Bodhi" enumerates their names.
"Because all marks are extinguished" explains and reveals the meaning of quiescence.
There are two kinds of extinction:
first, extinction by nature, which is fundamentally non-existent in reality; [second, extinction through cultivation].
Second is cessation through antidotes; one begins to depart from them only upon seeing reality.
Because of seeing reality, one realizes that delusion was originally non-existent and will not arise again; thus, all marks are extinguished.
In the subsequent phrases, the absence of characteristics is uniform throughout.
The following two phrases—“not contemplating” and “not practicing”—reveal the aforementioned universal quiescence;
therein, the first phrase clarifies the absence of contemplative understanding, while the latter clarifies the absence of the cultivation of practice.

In the preceding section on "Non-Contemplation" (*abhipaśyana*), the term is listed as a name; because false appearances arise from conditions and contemplation, yet these are fundamentally non-existent within the Truth, it is called "non-contemplation.
Furthermore, the realization of abandonment and relinquishment is also termed "non-contemplation"; this is an explanation based on the departure from conditions.
Contemplating and understanding the principle of conditions is termed "conditioning" (pratyaya);
realizing that which is fundamentally non-existent in truth is termed "detachment" (viveka).
Furthermore, the realization of abandonment and relinquishment is also termed "detachment."

In the section on "Clarifying Non-Practice," the term "non-practice" is listed as a heading. Cultivating the various *pāramitās* through conditions is called "practice"; because these are fundamentally non-existent within reality (*tattva*), it is termed "non-practice."
Furthermore, the realization of equanimity is also called "non-activity.
This is explained as "absence of recollection.
All conditioned phenomena arise from recollection; because there is no recollection, they do not proceed.
The following four lines explain and clarify the preceding points of non-contemplation and non-practice.
