second, Vimalakīrti’s refusal to accept it.
Third, the noble Sudatta practiced giving with a vast mind;
fourth, the householder Vimalakīrti received it.
Regarding the first point, "At that time, my mind attained purity," this refers to the purity of mental action (manas-karma).
To hear what was previously explained and to believe and delight in it without doubt is called "purity of mind.
To "marvel at what has never occurred before" is the vocal action of praise.
"Bowing one's head in worship," and so forth, is the physical action of prostration.
This is the skillful means of giving; it is the practice of giving at a low level.

As for the passage, "He immediately untied his necklace worth hundreds of thousands and offered it, yet [Vimalakīrti] refused to accept it," this refers to the second stage of Vimalakīrti’s non-acceptance.

Because he was biased in his reverence and restricted his giving solely to Vimalakīrti, his mind lacked the breadth to embrace others, thereby contradicting the principle of equal giving; this is why he did not accept.

When [the Buddha] said, "I say, householder, you must certainly accept it and take whatever is given according to your wish," this third section clarifies that his virtuous qualities consist in a broad mind that practices giving.
Because he did not accept [the gift] due to his specific restriction, [the donor] gave it according to his own will.
From this point downward is the fourth section, "Vimāna-datta Accepts.

First, he accepts it; then, from the phrase "dividing it into two" downward, he uses it for the purpose of further giving. Because he desires to teach people through material wealth and so forth, he performs this transference of the gift.
Within this, first the wealth is divided into two portions; subsequently, one is used for giving to others.
"One portion is given to the lowly beggars in this assembly"—giving to those who are lowly is equivalent to giving to those who are superior.
"One part is offered to that Tathāgata Duṣprasaha"—this refers to giving from the superior to the inferior.
"At that time, Vimalakīrti manifested supernatural transformations"—from this point downward, he instructs others based on his own example.
Regarding the phrase "Having manifested these supernatural transformations, he spoke thus," this reiterates what preceded to introduce what follows.
"If a donor" identifies the person being exhorted.

"Giving even to one of the lowest status, regarding them as having the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s field of merit and making no distinctions" is the actual instruction on how to practice giving.
"Equal to great compassion and seeking no reward" reiterates what was previously taught.
The Buddha is great compassion; when one's giving is equal to that of the Buddha, it is called "equal to great compassion."
To practice giving to the Tathāgata without partiality toward the karmic fruit is called "not seeking for fruit.
"This is what is called being fully endowed with the gift of Dharma" is the concluding praise intended to encourage study.
This concludes the third section.
The passage beginning with "In the city, one... constitutes the fourth section, clarifying the benefits of the gift of Dharma.
The phrase "In the city, [one] begs" identifies the person who receives the benefit.
"Seeing this supernatural power and hearing what was said" refers to the source from which benefit is derived.
Seeing the necklace previously bestowed by Vimalakīrti transform into a jeweled pavilion atop the Buddha Duṣprasaha is called "seeing the supernatural power."
Regarding the statement that "hearing [the Dharma] and making offerings to those of lower status equal to the Tathāgata, without seeking karmic retribution," this refers to what has been explained.
The phrase "all resolve their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*" precisely clarifies the attainment of benefit.
If only one person has resolved their mind [on enlightenment], why say "all"?
This resolution is the same as that mentioned previously; therefore, it is said "all.
Furthermore, it may also be because both seeing and hearing [the Dharma] trigger the resolution simultaneously; for this reason, it is said "all."
The preceding section provides the introduction, the subsequent section offers the explanation, and the passage beginning with "Therefore, I" concludes the discourse.
The address to the four individuals is listed separately by Ānanda;
the address to the remaining bodhisattvas, beginning with "In this way, each of these bodhisattvas turned toward," is summarized by Ānanda.
The full enumeration would be inexhaustible; therefore, they are mentioned collectively.
The text simply states "these bodhisattvas," without specifying how many there are.
They may perhaps be the thirty-two thousand bodhisattvas previously listed, or they may be the eight thousand bodhisattvas who later proceeded toward Vimalakīrti’s house.
Because their virtue was so exalted, everyone said they were incapable [of the task].

5. "The Chapter on Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry after Illness" (2b–3a): Regarding the "Chapter on Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry after Illness," previously all those addressed had declined, saying they were incapable; here, Mañjuśrī is commanded to go and inquire after his illness. Because this serves as the title for the chapter, it is named "The Chapter on Mañjuśrī’s Inquiry after Illness."
The first three sentences of this chapter are analyzed as follows:
first, the explanation of the purpose;
second, the differentiation from what precedes.
Third, the explanation by dividing the text.
Regarding the purpose of [Vimalakīrti’s] coming, there are three distinct intentions:
first, because Vimalakīrti’s virtue was so exalted that he was difficult to oppose and others were entirely unable to withstand him, he summoned Mañjuśrī and commanded him to go and inquire.
Second, because the Dharma to be elucidated is so sublime that others are unable to request it, it was necessary to command Mañjuśrī to go and inquire;
third, because the sentient beings to be transformed would find benefit by hearing the dialogue between these two individuals, it was necessary to command Mañjuśrī to inquire after his illness.
The purpose of [this section] is as follows.
Regarding the "distinguishing of differences," there are five types of distinctions, which have been fully explained above.

As for the "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*), the previous statement regarding his incapacity was made to manifest that Vimalakīrti’s personal virtue is so exalted and superior that it surpasses all other sages.
This address to those who are capable serves to manifest the wondrousness of his virtue; since only Mañjuśrī is capable, his virtue is indeed wondrous.
Regarding the second meaning: the previous address to those who were incapable served to manifest that Vimalakīrti’s eloquence was invincible, thereby revealing the superiority of his wisdom;
the subsequent address to those who are capable extensively reveals that Vimalakīrti’s spiritual transformations are unfathomable, thereby manifesting the superiority of his supernormal powers.

Regarding the third meaning: previously, when it was declared that [the disciples] were incapable, various words were extensively employed through others to manifest the virtue of Vimalakīrti’s liberation;
here, in contrast, for those who are capable, Vimalakīrti himself manifests the virtue of his liberation.
Regarding the fourth meaning: previously, for those who were deemed incapable, the Dharma taught by Vimalakīrti in the past was extensively revealed;
here, for those who are capable, the Dharma taught by Vimalakīrti in the present is extensively revealed.
Regarding the fifth meaning: the preceding section addressed those who were deemed incapable, thereby clarifying the essential nature of the Dharma studied by Bodhisattvas;
the subsequent section addresses those who are capable, revealing the characteristics of its cultivation and realization.
Such is the differentiation.
Next, the third section provides a detailed analysis and explanation.
This text is divided into two parts:
first, the introductory narrative concerning the instruction to Mañjuśrī to go inquire after his illness.
2. From "Welcome" (*svāgata*) onwards, the text correctly addresses the questioner and extensively expounds what was said.
Within the preceding section, starting from "The Tathāgata issues his command," it demonstrates Mañjuśrī receiving the command and proceeding to inquire.
The text is divided into four parts:
first, praising Vimalakīrti’s sublime virtue as being difficult to rival, and thus going to inquire after him by relying on [the Buddha’s] power;
second, proceeding together with the great assembly.
Third, Vimalakīrti knew [Mañjuśrī] was coming and waited for him in an empty room;
fourth, when Mañjuśrī arrived, he saw that the room was empty and [Vimalakīrti] was sleeping alone.
Within the first section, [the author] first praises Vimalakīrti to demonstrate that he himself is no match for his opponent.
From the words "Although... onwards, he proceeds to pose his question by relying on [the Buddha's] power.
Within the eulogy, the initial statement, "That superior person is difficult to engage in dialogue," is a general eulogy.
"Profoundly penetrating the true reality" marks the specific section.
Within this specific section, there are three parts:
first, praising Vimalakīrti’s superior wisdom and understanding;
2. From "Knowledge of all Bodhisattva methods" onwards, the perfection of practice and cultivation is shown;
3. From "Subduing Māra" onwards, the mastery of virtuous functions is shown.
Regarding the explanation within the "Exclamations," "profoundly penetrating the true reality" refers to what is called both actual wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*sākṣāt-kāra-jñāna*).

According to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, that which is termed conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) may be called true reality, or that which is termed ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) may be called true reality.
In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, the term "ultimate truth" (*paramārtha*) is frequently designated as "true reality" (*bhūtanimitta*).
Here, too, the "ultimate meaning" (*paramārtha*) should likewise be termed "true reality," for it is called "profound penetration" because it exhaustively realizes that which is real.

"Skillfully expounding the essential points of the Dharma" refers to the wisdom of skillful means, also called the wisdom of instruction; it is termed "skillful exposition" because it is able to proclaim the transformative teaching of the Dharma, and what is taught is termed "essential points" because they are truly significant.
"Unimpeded eloquence" (*pratibhāna*) clarifies the aforementioned skillful preaching.
Because one is able to discern and understand, and because one's speech is capable and dexterous, it is called "eloquence.
Because this eloquence flows smoothly and without obstruction, it is termed "unimpeded."
"Unimpeded wisdom" reveals the profound penetration mentioned previously; because one is able to enter into the profound, it is called "unimpeded.
Within the section on the perfection of practice, "knowing all the ritual methods of Bodhisattvas" refers to the excellence of one's own stage (*svabhūmi*).
"The secret treasury of all Buddhas is such that there is nothing one cannot enter" refers to the perfection of supreme cultivation.

Within the Great Nirvāṇa, the distinct gateways of the Dharma-realm are termed the "secret treasury of the Buddhas"; because one observes them exhaustively in accordance with reality, there is nothing into which one does not enter.
In various sutras, praises of virtue mostly rely upon these two.
Within the "Mastery of Virtue," "subduing all māras" refers to the virtue of destroying the heterodox,
while "sporting with supernatural powers" and so forth refer to the virtue of abiding in the correct.
"Playing with supernatural powers" (*vikrīḍita-abhijñā*) means mastery over the supernormal faculties.
Because one traverses all the supernormal powers with the ease of play, it is called "playing.
"Both his wisdom and skillful means have already reached the further shore" means that his wisdom is perfected.
Wisdom is true wisdom, and its skillful means is the wisdom of expedient methods.
When these two reach their ultimate fulfillment, they are said to have "crossed over.
Thus far, the sublime virtues of Vimalakīrti have been extensively praised.
From "Although" onwards, [the author] proceeds to pose questions by relying on [the Buddha’s] power.
The preceding section demonstrated that [the Buddha's answers] were difficult to repay; this section clarifies that by relying on [the Buddha’s] power, it is permissible to ask questions.
To distinguish between difficulty and ease, both are expressed using the phrase "although."
Nevertheless, it remains so.
Although he is difficult to confront, I have always followed the holy instructions of the Buddha to go and inquire.
To "receive from below" the power of that which is "above" is called "receiving" (承); "instructions" (旨) refers to the intended meaning.
This refers to going forth to inquire [about the matter] by receiving the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s power.
From this point downward is the second section, concerning Mañjuśrī’s departure together with the assembly.
Within this, there are three phrases:
First, clarifying that the assembly is mindful of the two Great Beings who will surely preach the sublime Dharma, the text first identifies those capable of such mindfulness:
"In this assembly. This is a general reference to the location, meaning within the assembly of the Buddha Āmra.
The phrase "all bodhisattvas" and so forth categorizes them according to their respective groups.
"All bodhisattvas" refers to the assembly of bodhisattvas;
"great disciples" refers to the assembly of śrāvakas.
The phrase "Śakra, Brahmā, and the kings" and so forth refers generally to the assembly of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The subsequent passage clarifies their thoughts.
"They all formed this thought" serves as the general heading.
"Xian" (咸) means "all.
The phrase "the two gentlemen now," etc., specifically identifies the persons being contemplated.

Because their great wisdom and lofty speech must be profound and far-reaching, [the Buddha] contemplates that these two Great Beings, in their conversation, will surely discourse upon the wondrous Dharma.
2. From "At that moment" onwards, it clarifies how the aforementioned assembly joyfully desired to follow.
3. From "Thereupon" onwards, it describes Mañjuśrī proceeding together with the assembly.
"In this regard, Mañjuśrī" refers to the leader of the assembly.
"Together with the various bodhisattvas and great disciples" enumerates his followers.
"Respectfully surrounding him" illustrates the manner of his departure.
"Entering Vaiśālī" distinguishes the destination reached.
From this point downward is the third section, wherein Vimalakīrti, knowing that the room was empty, awaits his arrival.
Within this, he first thinks, "Mañjuśrī is coming with the assembly"; he contemplates their arrival, not the empty room.
Some say: "This thought of wishing for an empty room serves as a cause for what follows.

This statement is erroneous; it is because Vimalakīrti awaited the transformation [of the Buddha] with the urgency of one who thirsts, and because the Tathāgata’s heart was filled with joy, that he formed this thought.

Next, regarding the passage "By his supernormal power he emptied the interior of the room, removing all possessions as well as the attendants": "emptying the room" is the general statement, while "removing the possessions and the attendants" clarifies how the room was made empty.
Wishing to provide a starting point for subsequent discourse, he therefore "emptied" [the room].

By stating that "he placed a single bed and lay upon it due to illness," he likewise wished to manifest something by means of his sickness; thus, he placed a single bed and manifested lying there as if ill.
From here below is the fourth section: Mañjuśrī’s journey to Śrāvastī and his entry into the house where he sees the emptiness [of the household]. He beholds only Vimalakīrti sleeping alone.
The preceding introduction is concluded.
From here below begins the formal exposition.
However, the distinction between the introductory (xiù) and the main (zhèng) sections is not fixed, as has been fully demonstrated above.
If one were to regard everything spoken by Vimalakīrti during his single lifetime as the orthodox teaching (zhèngzōng), that would be a partial judgment.

The first part, the "Chapter on Expedient Means" (Upāya-kauśalya-parivarta), serves as the introduction; from the passage, "Because of his illness, the kings and great ministers all went to inquire after his health," onwards, it constitutes the entire main body of the teaching (samyak-siddhānta).

If one takes what is currently being taught in this single assembly by Vimalakīrti as the definitive teaching, then everything from the preceding "Expedient Means" chapter onward would all be judged as the introduction to this assembly;
from this point forward, it would then constitute the main body of the teaching.
Within this main body of the text, there is a threefold analysis:
first, subsuming the teachings under the person to manifest their virtues and distinguish their categories;
second, setting aside the person to follow the teachings, distinguishing them according to their meaning.
3. Correct Interpretation Based on the Text.
Regarding how the teaching is subsumed under the person to manifest his virtues:
this sūtra’s primary theme is to manifest the virtues of Vimalakīrti; "virtues" refers to the gates of inconceivable liberation.

Within this section, the distinctions in meaning are as numerous as grains of dust; yet, when discussing them according to their merits, the essentials are simply the supremacy of wisdom (*jñāna*) and the supremacy of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

Above, the extensive citations from Vimalakīrti’s discourse have manifested the supremacy of his wisdom; below, the manifestation of Vimalakīrti’s sovereign spiritual transformations clarifies the supremacy of his supernormal powers.
The general [structure] is divided into four pairs according to their respective meanings:
from the beginning up to the "Inconceivable" chapter constitutes the first pair;
the "Contemplating Sentient Beings" chapter constitutes the second pair.
The "Chapter on the Buddha-way" constitutes the third pair;
from the "Gate of Non-duality" up to the "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation" constitutes the fourth pair.
In all four of these, the former portion clarifies what is practiced, while the latter portion reveals what is accomplished.
Within the first pair of chapters, the initial "Inquiry into the Illness" (*Vyādhikathana*) clarifies his practice;
the "Inconceivable" (*Acintya*) chapter clarifies his realization by means of Vairocana’s lamp-king throne and the small room’s vast capacity.
Within the second pair, the *Chapter on Examining Birth* first clarifies that which is practiced;

from the passage "At that time, there were goddesses in Vimalakīrti’s chamber" onwards, it demonstrates that Vimalakīrti’s chamber possesses the eight unprecedented qualities, thereby clarifying that which is accomplished.
Within the third pair of sections, the opening of the "Chapter on the Buddha-way" clarifies what he practices;
from the passage beginning with "simultaneously appearing to answer questions," it extensively reveals Vimalakīrti’s virtues in all their aspects, thereby manifesting what he has accomplished.
Within the fourth pair, the "Entrance into Nonduality" clarifies what is practiced;
the "Gandhavyūha" chapter clarifies what is accomplished by taking the fragrant seeds of the rice and the small room’s vast capacity.
What distinguishes these four pairs?

The first three pairs clarify the practice of the teachings (*śāsana-caryā*), wherein there is that which is cultivated and that which is accomplished; the final pair clarifies the practice of realization (*adhigama-caryā*), wherein there is that which is accomplished.

Regarding the first three among the latter [three], the first clarifies that the practice for remedying faults achieves its fruition; the latter two clarify that the practice of gathering wholesome qualities achieves its fruition.

Within the "Compendium of Wholesome Conduct," the first section clarifies the practice of entering quiescence and its accomplishment: relinquishing existence and contemplating emptiness is the entry into quiescence.
The subsequent section clarifies the practice of arising function and its accomplishment: acting upon what is not the path is the arising of function.
Thus, in the first gate, the teachings are subsumed under persons to manifest their virtues.
Next, in the second gate, persons are set aside in favor of the teachings, which are analyzed according to their meaning.

Although the meanings of the teachings expounded are immeasurable, they are essentially comprised of only cause and effect: "cause" refers to the causes of the *dharmakāya* and the pure land, and "effect" refers to the results of the *dharmakāya* and the pure land.

From the preceding "Expedient Means" chapter, where the kings and ministers all went to inquire after his illness because of his ailment, up to the end of the "Non-duality" chapter, the causes and conditions of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body are elucidated;
in the single chapter on "Fragrant Accumulation," the causes and conditions of the Tathāgata’s Pure Land are elucidated.
Regarding the clarification of the Dharma-body, it is divided into three parts according to its manifestations.

First, at the end of the preceding "Chapter on Expedient Means," because of the question regarding illness posed by an ordinary person, the causes and conditions for the Dharma-body of ordinary beings are clarified through the teaching.
"Delighting in the Buddha-body" refers to the fruit of the *dharmakāya*.
"Arising from immeasurable merits," and so forth, clarifies the causes of the *dharmakāya*.

In the second section, within the "Chapter on Disciples," the causes and fruits of the *śrāvaka* *dharmakāya* are clarified: for the preceding nine types of persons, the causes of the *dharmakāya* are clarified; for the final one type of person, the fruit of the *dharmakāya* is clarified.

From the third chapter, "The Bodhisattva’s Inquiry into the Illness," down to the end of the "Chapter on Non-duality," the teaching clarifies the causes and effects of the Dharma-body for bodhisattvas. The preceding section, in response to Maitreya, clarified the fruit of the Dharma-body; the true nature of bodhi is that fruit.
From the section on Prabhāvyūha onwards, it clarifies the causes of the Dharma-body; within these causes, the previous chapter elucidated the essence of their practice.
Following this chapter, the characteristics of cultivation and realization are elucidated; therein, they are briefly distinguished by way of two gates:
first, the distinction through the deconstruction of characteristics, and second, the distinction through the manifestation of virtues.
There are three aspects to the destruction of marks (*lakṣaṇa-vibhāga*):

from this point until the end of the "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings" constitutes the first division, wherein one practices cultivation to enter quiescence and destroys the marks of ordinary beings who cling to existence.
Second, the chapter "Buddha-Way" (*Fódào*) functions from the perspective of dependent origination to refute and abandon the attachment to emptiness characteristic of the two vehicles.
Third, the chapter "The Gate of Non-duality" (*Bù'èrmén pǐn*) realizes entry into non-duality to refute and eliminate the bodhisattvas' discrimination between dualistic marks.
The refutation of marks is thus.
Within the gateway of manifesting virtue, the essential contents are subsumed under two parts:

from the beginning up to the end of the "Buddha-way" chapter (*Fódǎo pǐn*), one practices the teachings and conduct based on the marks of liberation as explained by Vimalakīrti; in the "Non-duality" chapter (*Bù'èrmén pǐn*), one practices the realization and conduct based on the nature of liberation as explained by Vimalakīrti.
Within the preceding teachings on practice, there are three distinct pairs of meanings:

from the beginning up to the "Inconceivable" chapter constitutes the first pair; the "Contemplation of Sentient Beings" chapter constitutes the second pair; and the single chapter "The Buddha-way" constitutes the third pair.
Within these three pairs, the first again clarifies what is practiced and the latter clarifies what is accomplished, all as previously determined.
How do these three pairs differ?
The former two pertain to self-perfection (*svabhāva*), while the latter one pertains to superior progress (*viśeṣa*).
Cultivating the bodhisattva-dharma is called "self-benefit" (svabhāga), while seeking the Buddha-way above is called "superior progress" (viśeṣagamana).
Furthermore, the former two cultivations involve entering into the practice of quiescence, whereas the latter one clarifies the cultivation of the practice of manifesting activity.
"Engaging in what is not the Path" refers to the arousal of activity (*vyāpāra*).
To distinguish this according to the stages (*bhūmi*): entry into quiescence (*śamatha*) occurs mostly from the sixth stage downward, because of the delight in emptiness (*śūnyatā*);
the arousal of activity occurs mostly from the seventh stage upward, because there one cultivates the initiation of sublime practices (*viśeṣa-caryā*).

In the preceding section, first, there was accomplishment through the practice of purifying faults as clarified therein; subsequently, there was accomplishment through the practice of gathering wholesome qualities as clarified therein.
To briefly distinguish them by stage: practices that remedy faults are mostly found prior to the [ten] stages (*bhūmi*), because faults are heavy before the stages and must be remedied and severed;
practices that encompass virtues are mostly found from the first stage upward, because these practices accord with the *dharmadhātu* and bring about all spiritual qualities.

Within the first pair, the practice is explained first and the accomplishment is explained afterward; the practice occurs prior to the multiple stages, while the accomplishment occurs upon the multiple stages.
All of this clarifies the Dharma so as to lead people to study it.
This rough explanation of the "Discourse on the Abolition of Persons" concludes here.
End of the second fascicle of the *Vimalakīrti-arthavyākhyāna*.
